deep.reconstruction:
Context from the previous page: Hilbert has a theorem ('mein Satz') that certain discontinuous functions on [0,1] can be expanded in a series of polynomials sum_n (G_n - G_{n-1}) that converges at every point. His method:

(i) Choose a sequence of nodes x_1, x_2, ... dense in [0,1].
(ii) Let Z_n be the polygon ('Zickzacklinie') through the points (0, f(0)), (x_i, f(x_i)) for i <= n, and (1, f(1)).
(iii) By Weierstrass/Runge, pick polynomials G_n with |G_n - Z_n| < eps_n uniformly, where eps_n -> 0.
(iv) Then f(x) = G_1 + (G_2 - G_1) + (G_3 - G_2) + ...

Implicit justification (mine): the n-th partial sum is G_n. At a node x_k we have Z_n(x_k) = f(x_k) for all n >= k, so G_n(x_k) -> f(x_k). At a point x where f is continuous, the neighbouring nodes of x in Z_n tend to x as n grows, because the nodes are dense. Z_n(x) lies between f-values at those neighbours, so Z_n(x) -> f(x). Hence the series converges to f at every node and every continuity point. If f is discontinuous elsewhere, convergence may fail there.

The first example (previous page) is Thomae's function: f(p/q) = 1/q and f(irrational) = 0. Its discontinuity set is exactly the rationals.

This page:
(1) Hilbert claims the expansion exists whenever f has a point of continuity in every subinterval, i.e. the continuity points are dense. His parenthetical reason: then the set of discontinuities is countable ('Zahl' corrected to 'Menge'). One then takes as nodes all discontinuity points plus a dense countable set of continuity points. The construction above then gives everywhere convergence.
(2) Third example: Cantor's one-to-one map of a line segment onto a square (1878). Read coordinatewise, it is claimed to admit such an expansion.
(3) 'By the same principles' one can build a series of polynomials converging at every rational x and diverging at every irrational x.
(4) Open question: split each polynomial term into its monomials, keeping the order, giving a series of single powers a_k x^{e_k}. Does that series still converge like the first? The next page continues: if so, one obtains a fixed universal sequence 1; 1, x; 1, x, x^2; 1, x, ... such that every function of the class equals sum a_k G_k (no regrouping allowed).
errors: The key claim is false: dense continuity points do NOT imply a countable discontinuity set. Counterexample: the indicator of the Cantor set C. It is continuous on the dense open set [0,1]\C but discontinuous at all uncountably many points of C. (By Baire, the discontinuities of a function with dense continuity points form a meagre F_sigma set, not necessarily a countable one.)

Even as a criterion the statement is wrong: dense continuity points do not suffice for an everywhere-convergent polynomial expansion. Take f = 0 off C, and on C let f be 1 on a countable dense subset of C and 0 elsewhere. Continuity points are dense, but f restricted to the perfect set C has no continuity point. So f is not Baire class 1, and no pointwise convergent polynomial series exists (Baire 1899).
What Hilbert's argument correctly proves is: if the set of discontinuities is countable, then f is a pointwise limit of polynomials. Thomae's function falls under this.

The Cantor-bijection example is unjustified as stated. The interleaving-of-digits map has countably many discontinuities per coordinate. Cantor's actual 1878 bijection (continued fractions plus a countable reshuffling) needs separate analysis.

The splitting question (4) is left open. Naive splitting can fail: the intermediate monomial partial sums of a polynomial term can be huge. Example: the terms of (1-x)^n at x = 1. The remedy (mine): replace each block P_n by N_n copies of P_n/N_n with N_n large. Since |partial monomial sums| <= sum|c_k| on [0,1], the extra oscillation becomes small. So the answer is affirmative, with zero coefficients allowed in the universal sequence.

results.what: Everywhere-convergent polynomial series (via polygonal interpolation plus Weierstrass approximation) for functions with countably many discontinuities, e.g. Thomae's function
results.modern_name: Functions with countable discontinuity set are Baire class 1 (pointwise limits of polynomials)
results.usually_credited_to: Baire (1899); polygon technique cf. Runge 1885, Lebesgue 1898

results.what: Claimed criterion: a point of continuity in every interval suffices (with the wrong lemma that the discontinuity set is then countable)
results.modern_name: Incorrect precursor of Baire's characterization (Baire 1 iff every perfect set has a relative continuity point)

results.what: Series of polynomials convergent exactly on the rationals
results.modern_name: Convergence sets of sequences of continuous functions are exactly the F_sigma-delta sets (here Q, an F_sigma)
results.usually_credited_to: Hahn / Sierpinski / W.H. Young, c. 1910-1920 (unsure of precise attribution)

results.what: Splitting polynomial series into a monomial series with a universal ordering 1;1,x;1,x,x^2;...
results.modern_name: Representation by series of powers in fixed order (related to universal series, Pál/Fekete 1914)

deep.surprise_reason: The notebook dates to the late 1880s (it cites Runge 1885 and Minkowski 1887). It shows Hilbert explicitly studying everywhere-convergent polynomial series for discontinuous functions, a polynomial series convergent exactly on Q, and a universal monomial ordering. These are Baire-class-1 and convergence-set themes usually associated with Baire (1899) and later authors. However, his stated criterion is wrong and the material is exploratory, so it is a notable unpublished detail rather than a priority-changing result.
